history.heading: The Bounty mutineers
paragraphs: The Pitcairn Islands are a group of four volcanic islands in the South Pacific; only Pitcairn Island is inhabited. Polynesians lived there centuries earlier but had left before Europeans arrived. British navigator Philip Carteret sighted it in 1767.

In 1790 mutineers from HMS Bounty, led by Fletcher Christian, settled there with Tahitian men and women, burned their ship, and hid from the Royal Navy. Violence soon killed most of the men. The community was discovered by an American ship in 1808. Pitcairn became a British colony in 1838, one of the first territories to give women the vote.

history.heading: Modern Pitcairn
paragraphs: Overcrowding led many islanders to move to Norfolk Island in 1856, though some returned. In 2004 several men were convicted of sexual abuse of minors, a case that deeply affected the community.

culture.heading: The smallest community
paragraphs: Pitcairn has fewer than 50 residents, making it the least populous national jurisdiction in the world. Residents speak English and Pitkern, a creole of 18th-century English and Tahitian. Most are Seventh-day Adventists. Supplies arrive by ship from New Zealand a few times a year, and Adamstown is the only settlement.

politics.heading: British Overseas Territory
paragraphs: Pitcairn is a British Overseas Territory administered by a governor based in New Zealand, with a small elected Island Council. The government seeks new settlers to sustain the ageing population.

economy.heading: Small-scale economy
paragraphs: The economy relies on British aid, the sale of postage stamps, honey, handicrafts and the .pn internet domain, as well as tourism from occasional cruise ships. The surrounding waters form one of the world's largest marine protected areas. The currency is the New Zealand dollar.
